meta.title: Dying to Be Kind
meta.logline: When Mayor Hart cranks the town's Empathy Dial to eleven, Penny Doormat has to save her too-nice dad, her fridge and her whole town by learning when kindness helps and when it backfires.
meta.source: Ideas from 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), plus published criticism of the book (The Bulwark, Quillette).
meta.disclaimer: Parody and commentary. Original characters. Not affiliated with any author, network or show.

mayor.name: Mayor Marigold Hart
mayor.role: Feelings-first mayor; if it feels good, it's law

penny.name: Penny Doormat
penny.role: 10-year-old skeptic; asks the questions the audience is thinking

bounds.name: Dr. Hal Bounds
bounds.role: Evolutionary behavioral scientist; carries the book's thesis

kindt.name: Dr. Iris Kindt
kindt.role: Compassion researcher; carries the critics' counterpoint

rocco.name: Rocco
rocco.role: A raccoon who has never heard the word no

lines.text: Good evening, Kindleton! I'm Ken Brightside, and tonight the nicest town on Earth gets even nicer.
Live from Town Square, Mayor Marigold Hart unveils her greatest invention yet.
Citizens! For too long, our kindness has been held back by one terrible thing. Thinking.
Behold! The Municipal Empathy Dial!
Today, we crank it all the way to eleven!
Woo hoo! I can feel my feelings feeling things!
Dad, the dial only goes to ten. Eleven is literally labeled, uh oh.
Look, Penny! A raccoon at the door! Come in, little buddy. My fridge is your fridge.
*chitter chitter* (eats everything)
Dad, he just ate the lasagna, the plate, and the dog's birthday cake.
Penny, saying no to a raccoon is raccoon-phobic. I read it on a mug.
*jingle jingle* (takes the car keys)
He's taking the car keys.
He looks like a very responsible driver!
*VROOM... CRASH*
Okay. I need a grown up. A smart one.
Hello, Penny. Doctor Hal Bounds, evolutionary behavioral scientist, and fellow raccoon survivor.
First, let me be clear. Empathy is wonderful. It's an evolved instinct. It's why parents protect babies and strangers jump into rivers.
But any instinct can misfire. Gad Saad's book has a name for it: suicidal empathy. A virtue misfiring so badly it hurts the very people it means to protect.
Aristotle saw this coming. Virtue lives in the middle. Too little empathy, you get a psychopath. Too much, you get... your father.
So how exactly does it misfire?
Three ways. One, too much of it. Two, aimed at the wrong target. Three, feelings used where math belongs.
Picture a bridge engineer who asks the steel how it feels about holding weight.
In other news, Kindleton Elementary has abolished wrong answers. Two plus two now equals whatever makes you happy.
Feels great today. Next year, nobody can do their taxes.
Exactly. Saad calls it empathetic myopia. You only see the first domino.
Meanwhile, Councilman Chet Gatesworth, speaking from his gated mansion on Snob Hill, voted to remove the locks from every other house in town.
A luxury belief. It buys you status, while the bill gets mailed to somebody else.
And the Mayor announced the town's one and only goal: zero scraped knees. Sports, stairs and fun are now banned.
Single objective thinking. Measure only one thing, and you quietly trade away everything you forgot to measure.
My new post, I care more than you, just hit one million likes! Ooh, the dopamine! It feels so good, it must be good!
That's the trap. The reward comes from looking kind, not from the results of being kind.
Now, in the book Saad takes this into the hottest topics there are. Immigration, crime, campus speech, research people would rather not hear. That's exactly where his critics push back hardest.
So let's hear them out.
Tonight on Heart versus Head: is empathy killing us? On my left, Doctor Hal Bounds. On my right, compassion researcher Doctor Iris Kindt.
Hal, empathy built hospitals, helped end slavery, and feeds strangers every day. Too much kindness is hardly the West's biggest problem.
Agreed. Kindness isn't the disease. Uncalibrated kindness is. Feeling more for the arsonist than for the people in the burning building.
Here's my worry. Call something suicidal empathy, and you can slap that label on any policy you happen to dislike. Reviewers say the book does exactly that.
And the opposite failure is real too. Cruelty dressed up as being realistic has a body count of its own.
Fair. So don't argue about labels. Test the policy. Is it true? Who pays? And what happens next year?
I can live with that. Compassion, with receipts.
Wow. Two experts agreeing on live television. Folks, this has never happened.
Okay, Dad. New house rule. Three questions before every yes.
Is it true that Rocco is a licensed driver?
No.
Who pays for the car?
You do.
And what happens next year?
Rocco owns a car dealership. With your credit card.
Rocco, buddy. You can stay. But you wash the dishes.
*happy chitter* (grabs a sponge)
That's reciprocity. Kindness that can survive contact with reality.
So I'm turning my heart down?
No, Dad. You're turning your brain up.
Fine! If empathy is the problem, we'll crank it all the way down to zero!
Citizens. Kittens will now be taxed. By weight.
And that's the other ditch. Somewhere, Aristotle is spinning.
